subtype: Um, uh and filler in public speaking [Regulating]
passage: The conference hall was full and the projector hummed. Salma stepped up to give her first presentation on library funding. Her hands were damp, and she said, "Um, so, uh, thank you all for coming." She heard herself and stopped. Elizabeth, her mentor, in the front row, had told her once: pause instead. So Salma paused, breathed, looked at her notes and said, "Today I will share three findings." The room was quiet and attentive. The silence felt long to her, though probably only a moment. Later Elizabeth said, "Nobody noticed the um at the start. But the pause made you sound sure."

qa.q: What was Salma's presentation about?
qa.a: It was about library funding.

qa.q: How did Salma feel at the start of the talk, and what evidence suggests it?
qa.a: Salma was nervous, shown by her damp hands and the "um, so, uh" opening. The pause helped her steady herself.

qa.q: What could Salma try in her next talk?
qa.a: Salma could keep pausing and breathing instead of filling the gap with um and uh, as Elizabeth suggested.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have felt watching Salma pause?
qa.a: Elizabeth probably felt proud and reassured, since the pause made Salma sound sure.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional replacing um and uh with a pause during a presentation, which reads as more confident.

passage:
Dear Akash,

Thank you for coming to my talk, and for the feedback afterwards. You said I said "um" eleven times in the first minute, and I laughed, but it made me think. I practised at home with my phone recording and tried to replace each um with a short silence. It felt strange and long at first, as if the whole room would notice. But when I watched the video, the pause looked calm and thoughtful. I also learned that fillers do not mean I do not know my subject; I do, I was just nervous. I will try the pause at the department seminar next week. 🙂

Aparna

qa.q: What did Aparna practise with at home?
qa.a: Aparna practised with a phone recording.

qa.q: What did Aparna feel when the pause first felt long, and what did the video show?
qa.a: Aparna felt the silence was strange and long and worried the room would notice. The video showed the pause looked calm and thoughtful.

qa.q: What could Aparna do at the department seminar?
qa.a: Aparna could replace ums with short pauses and breaths, as practised.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt giving that feedback?
qa.a: Akash probably wanted to help and hoped Aparna would take it kindly, since the count was given as feedback and Aparna laughed.

grounding: Letter from a young professional who practises replacing um and uh with a pause while presenting.

subtype: Um, uh and filler in public speaking [Regulating]
passage: Dilnaz, you asked how the conference talk went. Better than the last one, which is saying something. Last time, a man in the second row actually counted my ums out loud to his friend: "Twenty-six." I heard him. I was so resentful I could barely finish, and for weeks I wondered whether I really knew my subject. But I did know it. The ums were just my brain buying time. So this time I practised in front of my bathroom mirror every evening for two weeks. Every time I felt an "um" coming, I closed my mouth and let one breath of silence sit there. At first it felt like forever. On the day, when I paused after the key result, the room actually leaned in. A few ums slipped out, and nobody cared. That's Dhruv's new trick: silence, not um.

qa.q: How many ums did the man in the second row count?
qa.a: Twenty-six.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel after hearing the ums counted aloud?
qa.a: Dhruv felt resentful and humiliated, and for weeks doubted knowing the subject, even though that knowledge was solid.

qa.q: What practice helped Dhruv, and why?
qa.a: Practising in front of a mirror for two weeks and replacing each 'um' with a breath of silence, which made pauses feel natural and let the audience lean in.

qa.q: How did the audience respond to Dhruv's pause this time?
qa.a: The room leaned in after the key result, and when a few ums slipped out, nobody cared.

grounding: A young professional recalls fillers being mocked, knowing they did not mean ignorance, and replacing them with short pauses.

subtype: Um, uh and filler in public speaking [Regulating]
passage: I'm Chaitanya, and I sit in on the Friday demos at our startup. When Divyansh joined in June, his demos were full of "um" and "uh", three or four in every sentence. Some people checked their phones. One senior developer muttered that he didn't understand his own code. I didn't agree; when you asked Divyansh a question afterwards, his answers were sharp. The ums seemed to come from nerves, not ignorance, though I can't be sure what was in his head. In August something changed. He'd reach a hard part, stop, look at the screen, and let a second or two of silence pass before speaking. The first few times it was so quiet you could hear the air conditioner. Then people started looking up from their phones during the pauses, waiting for the next line. Last Friday his demo got the first spontaneous clap I've heard in that room.

qa.q: When did Divyansh join?
qa.a: In June.

qa.q: What might Divyansh's many ums in June suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Most likely nervousness about presenting, since his answers afterwards were sharp; Chaitanya can't be sure, but it didn't look like ignorance.

qa.q: What did Divyansh change, and why did it work?
qa.a: He replaced fillers with a second or two of silence at hard parts, which made him seem more confident and drew attention to the next line.

qa.q: How did the senior developer read Divyansh's fillers?
qa.a: The senior developer took them as a sign Divyansh didn't understand his own code, misreading normal nervous fillers as ignorance.

grounding: An observer describes a young professional's fillers read as ignorance and his switch to short pauses making him seem more confident.

passage:
Thursday: Tushar played back the recording of Charu's rehearsal for the startup pitch. "Um, so, uh, our product, um, helps..." He had counted: thirty-one ums in four minutes. Charu covered her face. "I sound like I don't know what I'm talking about." "You know it better than anyone," Tushar said. "The ums are just nerves."
Saturday: They practised in his living room. Each time she felt an "um" coming, Charu pressed her lips shut and breathed once. The silences felt huge to her. Tushar timed them: barely two seconds. "From here it just sounds like you're thinking," he said.
The following Tuesday: At the pitch in the incubator's glass room, Charu reached the numbers slide, stopped, breathed, and let the silence sit. Three investors looked up from their notes. A few ums slipped in near the end, and nobody seemed to notice. Afterwards Tushar texted: "Four ums. FOUR."

qa.q: How many ums did Tushar count in the rehearsal?
qa.a: Thirty-one ums in four minutes.

qa.q: How did Charu feel hearing the recording on Thursday?
qa.a: Charu felt embarrassed and deflated, covering her face and fearing she sounded as if she didn't know her subject.

qa.q: What helped Charu cut the fillers?
qa.a: Practising with Tushar and replacing each 'um' with one breath of silence, which from outside just sounded like thinking.

qa.q: How did the investors react to Charu's pause at the numbers slide?
qa.a: Three investors looked up from their notes, suggesting the silence drew their attention rather than making her seem unsure.

grounding: Shows a young professional practising pauses in place of fillers over several days, with fillers treated as normal nerves, not ignorance.

passage:
Wasim, you're worried about the ums? Let me tell you about my first board presentation. Twelve people round a long table, and I said "um" so often that one director started tapping his pen every time. Tap. Um. Tap. I could hear it. I finished red in the face, sure they all thought Kunal knew nothing.
Afterwards my manager, Mrs. Fernandes, said, "Your numbers were solid. The ums don't mean you don't know. They mean you're scared of silence." She told me: when you feel an um coming, close your mouth, breathe, and let the room wait one second.
At the next board meeting I tried it. The pauses felt endless to me. But the same director told me later I seemed confident. The silence was helping them think too.
So, your ums are normal. Just try swapping a few of them for a breath.

qa.q: How many people were round the long table?
qa.a: Twelve people were round the long table.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel as the director tapped the pen?
qa.a: Kunal felt humiliated and anxious, red in the face, sure they all thought Kunal knew nothing.

qa.q: What turning point came at the next board meeting?
qa.a: Kunal replaced ums with a breath and a one-second pause, as Mrs. Fernandes suggested, and the director later read it as confidence. 🙂

qa.q: How did the director see the pauses at the later meeting?
qa.a: The director read them as confidence, and the silence gave the listeners time to think.

grounding: Replacing filler words with short pauses makes a speaker sound more confident, and fillers do not mean the speaker lacks knowledge.
